rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-11) <U+2014> the authors run their own HSPF model simulations of the 3.27 km2 Tumenxigou catchment driven by five bias-corrected GCMs under RCP 8.5, with the model calibrated and validated on 2014-2015 observed streamflow and water quality data from a previous study.
rows.notes: The study contains no remote sensing and no surface soil moisture retrieval; soil water content is an internal HSPF model output. It does not address crop yield forecasting or crop production at all. What it actually shows is that, under projected climate, heavy rain and rainstorm events following prolonged drought increase runoff, sediment, TN, TP and fecal coliform loads to a drinking-water catchment, with antecedent soil water content as an important interacting factor (multiple regression, Table 3). It therefore offers no own evidence on remote-sensing SSM products delivering crop-yield information.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-11) <U+2014> own HSPF model runs for the Tumenxigou catchment under five GCM projections (RCP 8.5), model previously calibrated/validated against 2014-2015 observations (Table S5).
rows.notes: The study does not use remote sensing or satellite soil moisture products; soil moisture is simulated by HSPF. It does not evaluate climate-resilient agricultural management or irrigation scheduling based on SSM retrieval. Its actual result is a model-based assessment of how drought followed by intense rainfall mobilises sediment, nutrients and fecal coliforms into a drinking-water source catchment, highlighting the role of antecedent soil moisture; it discusses adaptive watershed management only as a general implication. No own evidence for remote-sensing-based risk management.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a modelling study (HSPF + five CMIP5 GCMs) on watershed hydrology and nonpoint-source pollution; it has no remote-sensing component, so it cannot support either claim about remote-sensing SSM products. The review appears to cite it loosely for the general relevance of soil moisture to climate-resilient management.
